## Preliminaries

The libraries expected to be used are downloaded.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(repurrrsive)
```

These are the questions I set out to explore:

1)  List those who won more than once

2)  Filter men and women. Calculate the proportion of women and men winners

3)  Compare the proportion of men and women winners in economics against all the other disciplines combined.

4)  Filter and combine winners by science and by continent of birth. I am thinking of continent rather than country because I would like to create a table and with many countries, it will be difficult to read.

### The data

For this exercise data had to be requested from the Nobel Prize organization developer API. I was able to download the data and uploaded it in GitHub. From there I was able to retrieve them in R.

The Nobel Prize organization developer API provides two endpoints I have used both. I have explored their nested structure.

```{r}
Winners<- read_json("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Enrique01234/607-Fall-2026/refs/heads/main/Laurates2.json", simplifyVector = TRUE)
```

```{r}
NobelWinners<- read_json("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Enrique01234/607-Fall-2026/refs/heads/main/NobelWinners.json", simplifyVector = TRUE)
```

```{r}
##Winners
```

```{r}
##NobelWinners
```

I started with the data frame "Winners". I selected each winner's ID to start creating a data frame (Winners_id) to use for my analysis.

At this point I realized I did not have all the winners. I have tried several times to go back to the Nobel Prize API and retrieve all of them. I did manage to do so every time. However, when converting it to a JSON file, it got truncated every time, Nevertheless, I decided to continue with the exercise with a smaller set of winners (which hampered some of the questions I wanted to explore).

```{r}
Winners_id<-Winners$laureates|>
  select(id)
```

```{r}
Winners_id
```

The, I added some of the other variables I am interested in exploring.

```{r}
Winners_id<-Winners$laureates|>
  select(id, fileName, gender)
```

```{r}
Winners_id
```

Selecting these variables was rather straightforward. Selecting the continent the winners are from was more difficult, given the nested structure. So I created a different data frame (Winners_loc).

```{r}
Winners_loc<-Winners$laureates$birth$place$continent|>
    select(en)
```

```{r}
Winners_loc
```

In order to be able to join these two data frames, I created a new variable (newid) in each data frame.

```{r}
Winners_loc$newid <- 1:nrow(Winners_loc)
```

```{r}
Winners_id$newid <- 1:nrow(Winners_id)
```

Then I created a new data frame (Winners_idloc), basically replicating (Winners_id). to be used for joining the two data frames.

```{r}
Winners_idloc<- Winners_id
```

I did a simple inner-join.

```{r}
Winners_idloc<- Winners_idloc|> 
  inner_join(Winners_loc)
```

As the categories (sciences) for each winner were deeply nested in the data frame Winners (at least for me), I found it easier to retrieve them from the NobelWinners data frame.

```{r}
Winners_cat<-NobelWinners$nobelPrizes$category|>
  select(en)
```

```{r}
Winners_cat
```

However, these 25 entries are not the same as the 25 in the other data frame Thus, I cannot join them.

I know they are not the same because, when analyzing the structure, I can see the names are different.

I have also tried unnesting from the Winners data frame.

```{r}
Categories<-Winners
```

```{r}
Categories2<-tibble(tounnest = Categories)
```

```{r}
Categories2 |> unnest_wider(tounnest)
```

The list with the categories is there. I just could not find a way to retrieve it.

## The One Result

There are famous cases of persons who won more than one Nobel Prize (e.g. Marie Curie). However, I have used a truncated data set (he first 25 winners with first name starting with A). Thus, I did not find any repeat winner. I could not answer two of the remaining questions.

I could only answer (partially, as I had only 25 winners), the question about the proportion of women and men winners.

Grouping these winners by male and female is simple. Counting them and producing a bar graph to show them is also easy.

```{r}
Winners_idloc|>
  group_by(gender)|>
  count()
```

```{r}
ggplot(Winners_idloc, aes(x = gender)) + 
  geom_bar()
```

Identifying specifically the female winner is also easy.

```{r}
Winners_f<- Winners_idloc|>
  filter(gender == "female")
```

```{r}
Winners_f
```

Besides the count, the proportions of male and female winners can also be calculated.

```{r}
Winners_idloc |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  mutate(freq = n / sum(n))
```
